pages.title: CSS Box Model
pages.content:
- You've learned to style elements with colors, fonts, and borders. Now, it's time to understand the most fundamental concept in CSS: **The Box Model**.
- The Box Model explains how every single HTML element—from a `` to a `` tag—is treated as a rectangular box by the browser. This model determines an element's total size and how it takes up space on the page.
---
Think of it like a gift box with four layers:

1. **Content:** This is the innermost layer. It's the actual content of the element, such as your text or an image.
2. **Padding:** This is the empty space **inside** the box, between the content and the border. It's like the protective packing material that adds breathing room around the content.
3. **Border:** This is the line that wraps around the padding and content. It's the physical box itself.
4. **Margin:** This is the empty space **outside** the box. It separates the element from other elements on the page, like the empty space on a table between your gift box and another item.



---
**The order always goes from the inside out:**
`Content` → `Padding` → `Border` → `Margin`

- Understanding these four layers is key to controlling the size, spacing, and layout of every element on your web page.

pages.title: CSS Borders - Style Your Elements
pages.content:
- You've already used a simple `border` as part of the Box Model. You know it adds a line around an element. Now, let's look at how you can make your borders much more creative and interesting.
- Borders are made up of three parts: a **width**, a **style**, and a **color**. By changing these properties, you can create a wide variety of effects.

**Border Style**

This property is the most powerful. It defines what your border actually looks like. Some common styles are:

* `solid`: A single, solid line (the one you've used so far).
* `dotted`: A border made of dots.
* `dashed`: A border made of dashes.
* `double`: Two solid lines right next to each other.

---
**Border-Radius**
- This property is what you use to create rounded corners. Instead of a sharp, square corner, you can give your boxes soft, curved edges.
- The value of `border-radius` controls how much the corners are rounded. A larger number creates a more rounded corner. Using `border-radius: 50%` is a simple trick to create a perfect circle or oval from a square or rectangle.

By combining these properties, you can give your elements a professional and polished look.

```css
.notification { border: 2px solid #2563eb; border-radius: 8px; }
```

topics.title: Display Property and Colors
topics.description: Study concepts and solve targeted engineering problems for Display Property and Colors.

pages.title: CSS Display Property
pages.content:
- You have learned how to style your boxes with colors, padding, and borders. Now, let's learn how to control how those boxes arrange themselves on the page.
- The `display` property is one of the most important in CSS. It defines the fundamental "type" of an element, which controls how it acts in relation to other elements. Think of it as an element's basic rule for how it appears and takes up space.

---
Here are the four most common values:

* **`display: block;`** (The Stacker):
   * This is the default for elements like ``, ``, and ``.
   * Block elements always start on a **new line**.
   * They take up the **full available width** of their parent, like a giant invisible wall, forcing the next element below it.

* **`display: inline;`** (The Flow-er):
   * This is the default for elements like `` and ``.
   * Inline elements sit on the **same line** as other content.
   * They only take up as much width as their content needs.
   * **You cannot** set a `width` or `height` on an inline element.

* **`display: inline-block;`** (The Best of Both Worlds):
   * This is a special value that combines the best of both types.
   * Like an inline element, it sits on the **same line** as other elements.
   * But, like a block element, you **can** set a `width`, `height`, and all sides of `margin` and `padding`. This makes it a powerful tool for arranging elements side-by-side.

* **`display: none;`** (The Disappear-er):
   * This value makes an element completely **invisible**.
   * It removes the element from the page layout entirely, and it takes up **no space**.
---

pages.title: CSS - Height and Width
pages.content:
- You have learned to style the borders and spacing of your elements. Now, let's learn how to control their exact size.
- The `height` and `width` properties control how tall and how wide an element is. They are most commonly used on `block` and `inline-block` elements.
---
**Pixels (`px`)**\
This gives you a **fixed, exact size**. A `200px` width will always be 200 pixels wide, no matter the screen size. Use pixels when you need a very specific, unchanging dimension.

**Percentages (`%`)**\
This gives you a **flexible, relative size**. A percentage is based on the size of the element's parent container. For example, `width: 50%;` will make the element take up exactly half the width of the box it's inside.

**`auto`**\
This is the **default** value. It tells the browser to automatically calculate the size based on the element's content. For example, a paragraph's height will grow or shrink to fit all its text.

---

```css
.media { width: 100%; max-width: 480px; height: 240px; }
```

pages.title: CSS Overflow
pages.content:
- You have learned how to give your elements a specific `height` and `width`. But what happens when you put more content inside a box than it can hold? The content will overflow its container.
- The `overflow` property tells the browser what to do with this extra content. Think of it as deciding what to do with items that don't fit in a fixed-size box.

---
**Three Main Values for the Overflow Property**

**1.`overflow: hidden;`** (The Chopper)
- This value simply cuts off any content that goes beyond the edges of the container. The overflowing content will be invisible and completely inaccessible.
* **Use case:** When you want to ensure your layout stays clean and nothing spills outside of a specific area.

**2.`overflow: scroll;`** (The Scroller)
- This value adds a scrollbar to the container, whether the content needs it or not. The user can then scroll to see the hidden content.

* **Use case:** When you always want a scrollbar to appear in a certain area for a consistent design.

**3.`overflow: auto;`** (The Smart Scroller)
- This is the most common and often best choice. It is smart because it only adds a scrollbar **if and when** the content actually overflows the container.

* **Use case:** When you want to allow scrolling for long content without showing a scrollbar for short content, creating a cleaner look.

```css
.comments { max-height: 280px; overflow-y: auto; }
```

pages.title: CSS Backgrounds - Colors and Images
pages.content:
- When building a webpage, the **background** sets the tone and feel. CSS lets you change the background of any element using **solid colors** or **images**.

**1. `background-color`**: 
This property fills the background of an element with a solid color.

* You can use color names (`red`, `blue`), HEX codes (`#ff0000`), RGB (`rgb(255,0,0)`), or HSL (`hsl(0, 100%, 50%)`).

**Example:**

```css
p {
  background-color: lightblue;
}
```

This makes every paragraph have a light blue background.

---
**2. `background-image`**:
This property sets an image as the background of an element.

* The image repeats by default to fill the space.
* You can combine it with other properties (like `background-repeat`, `background-size`) to control how it looks.

**Example:**

```css
body {
  background-image: url("pattern.png");
}
```

This adds a repeating pattern image to the page background.
